1. Install Shizuku, or a Shizuku fork such as Shevery, and start it (Wireless debugging, then Start). It has to be started again after every reboot.
2. For a car, install AnyAuto with UnknownAuto: Android Auto only runs apps installed from Google Play. The desktop head unit doesn\'t check.
3. Choose the apps for the car. Try shows an app at car size on this phone. Tap the tune icon next to an app to set its own display DPI, orientation lock, or safe edge inset.

4. In the car, open AnyAuto and pick an app. AnyAuto\'s navigation bar runs down the left of the car screen: Back, Apps, Last, Keyboard, Close and Hide. To have it on the right, choose ⋮ → Navigation bar side.

5. On Xiaomi / HyperOS / MIUI phones, also enable \"USB debugging (Security settings)\" in Developer options so car touches and keys work, set Battery saver to No restrictions, turn on Autostart, and lock AnyAuto in Recents.
While an app is on the car screen

On many phones the car screen runs on its own and the phone is left alone: lock it or use it as usual. Where the car screen would sleep with the phone (Android 17 on a Pixel, for example), the phone stays awake with its screen off. The power button still puts it to sleep; the car screen then pauses until you tap it. When Android Auto stops showing AnyAuto, the phone goes back to how it was.
To use the phone at the same time, turn on ⋮ → Keep the phone\'s screen on.

If your phone turns its screen straight back on, or goes to sleep, when AnyAuto turns it off, AnyAuto stops doing that so the screen doesn\'t flicker, and turns on Keep the phone\'s screen on for later drives.

Tap a text field and the keyboard opens on the car screen. The Keyboard button opens it for the selected text field, or closes it. By default, AnyAuto briefly wakes the phone screen while the car keyboard is open so microphone voice dictation works; you can change this or move the keyboard to the phone in ⋮ → Keyboard.

Back is the app\'s own Back. Apps goes to the apps grid. Last switches directly between the two most recently used apps. Close closes the app, like swiping it away in Recents. Hide gives the app the whole width; the bar button at the top right of the car screen brings the bar back.
That bar button is Android Auto\'s own: it floats over the app until it hides, and a tap on the screen shows it again. To keep it out of the app\'s way, turn off ⋮ → Full screen in the car.
On Android 11 and newer, ⋮ → Split screen (Freeform) lets you open a second app alongside the first one in a 60/40 two-pane layout.

With a rotary knob or a touchpad, select Android Auto\'s pan button (✥) at the bottom right and press: a ring, AnyAuto\'s pointer, appears. Push the knob to move it; quick pushes go further. Press the knob to click where the ring is, and press the pan button again for the next click.

Push past the top or bottom edge to scroll. Push the ring into the navigation bar and it lands on a button; up and down go from button to button. The car\'s Back button is the app\'s Back, and once you have used the pointer, Android Auto\'s buttons include Apps too.
After 10 seconds without the knob, Android Auto hides its buttons and the ring goes away. The next press of the pan button then clicks nothing; press it again to bring the ring back.

No pan button? Some wireless adapters tell Android Auto that the car has a touch screen. Turn on ⋮ → Pointer buttons (knob): Android Auto\'s buttons get Pointer (push the knob up to reach them), which turns them into Tap, Done and four arrows. Press an arrow to move the ring (quick presses go further), then Tap to click there. An arrow at the edge scrolls, and Done brings the usual buttons back. After 10 seconds without the knob, the focus goes back to Tap.

When you open AnyAuto, it looks for a new version on GitHub. When one is ready, tap Update on the Home screen, then Install in UnknownAuto, so Android Auto keeps accepting AnyAuto. Nothing runs in the background. Turn it off with ⋮ → Check for updates automatically.
Apps that protect their windows (banking, DRM video, incognito tabs) show black.
